module_title: Incubation and Hatching: From Egg to Chick

lessons.title: Collecting and Storing Fertile Eggs for Hatching
lessons.body:
Collecting eggs for hatching starts with healthy breeding stock. Keep one male for every 3 to 5 female quail or guinea fowl. Feed them quality layer feed with 16-18% protein and plenty of clean water. Collect eggs at least twice a day, early morning and late afternoon, because eggs left in the sun or rain spoil quickly. Use clean hands or a soft cloth to pick eggs; never wash them with water because that removes the protective bloom that keeps bacteria out. If an egg is dirty, gently rub it with fine sandpaper or a dry cloth. Discard cracked, misshapen, or very small eggs.

Store eggs in a cool, dark place at 15-20Â°C (59-68Â°F) and 70-80% humidity. In hot African climates, a clay pot or a cardboard box with a damp cloth over it works well. Do not store eggs in a refrigerator; the cold kills the embryo. Keep eggs pointed end down in clean egg trays or cartons. Turn them at least twice a day by tilting the tray to a 45-degree angle. Eggs can be stored for up to 7 days for quail and 10 days for guinea fowl; after that, hatchability drops fast. Mark the date on each egg with a pencil so you know which are oldest.

For best results, set eggs that are between 1 and 5 days old. If you collect eggs over several days, store them in the same cool place and turn them daily. Avoid storing eggs near strong smells like kerosene or onions because eggshells absorb odours. Before setting eggs in the incubator or under a hen, let them warm to room temperature for 2-4 hours. This reduces condensation and improves hatch rates. Never set eggs that have been in the sun or over 10 days old. A simple notebook to record collection dates and storage conditions helps you track fertility and plan your hatch.

lessons.title: Natural Incubation: Using Local Hens or Guinea Fowl to Hatch Quail Eggs
lessons.body:
Natural incubation uses a broody hen or guinea fowl to keep eggs warm. A local hen that has stopped laying and sits on eggs for 21 days is broody. Guinea fowl can also hatch quail eggs, but they are often nervous. Choose a quiet, dark nest box lined with dry grass or soft cloth. Place the nest in a safe place away from other birds, rats, and snakes. A raised hut or a corner of a secure coop works well. Make sure the hen can leave once a day to eat, drink, and dust-bathe. Provide food and water nearby so she does not stay off the nest too long.

Quail eggs are small, so a hen can cover 15-20 quail eggs or 10-12 guinea fowl eggs. Do not mix eggs from different species because they hatch at different times. Mark each egg with a pencil date and set them under the hen at night. The hen will turn the eggs herself and keep them at about 37.5Â°C (99.5Â°F). Check the nest daily when the hen is off, removing any broken eggs. Do not disturb the hen too much; stress can make her abandon the nest. If the hen is sitting tight, she will only leave once or twice a day for 15-20 minutes.

Hatch day for quail is 17-18 days, and for guinea fowl 26-28 days. Around day 15 for quail or day 24 for guinea fowl, stop turning the eggs and do not let the hen leave the nest as often. Listen for peeping and tapping sounds. Chicks will pip (break) the shell and emerge wet and tired. Do not help unless the chick is stuck for more than 12 hours. After hatching, leave chicks under the hen for 24 hours to dry. Then move them to a warm brooder with a heat lamp or a box with a 60-watt bulb. Natural incubation is cheap and needs no electricity, but it is slower and you cannot control the number of eggs. Always keep a backup plan like a low-cost incubator.

lessons.title: Building a Low-Cost Incubator with a Thermostat and Bulb
lessons.body:
You can build a simple incubator using a wooden box, a cardboard box, or a plastic cooler. The box should be at least 40 cm long, 30 cm wide, and 30 cm high for 30-50 quail eggs. Line the inside with aluminium foil or reflective material to keep heat even. Cut a small window on the lid and cover it with clear plastic or glass so you can see inside without opening. Drill two small holes near the bottom for air flow and one near the top for a thermometer and humidity gauge. A cheap digital thermometer-hygrometer costs about $5 and is essential.

Heat comes from a 40-watt or 60-watt incandescent bulb. Do not use LED or energy-saving bulbs because they do not produce enough heat. Connect the bulb to a thermostat. A simple wafer thermostat from an old refrigerator or a cheap reptile thermostat works well. Set the thermostat to 37.5Â°C (99.5Â°F). Place the bulb at one end and the thermostat sensor near the eggs. Add a small fan from an old computer to circulate air, but if not available, keep the bulb low and the eggs not directly under it. Test the incubator for 24 hours before setting eggs. Adjust the bulb height or thermostat until the temperature stays steady between 37.2Â°C and 37.8Â°C.

For humidity, place a small plastic container of water inside. Aim for 45-55% humidity during incubation and 65-75% during the last 3 days. Add a sponge or cloth to increase humidity. Turn eggs by hand at least 4 times a day, or build an automatic turner using a small motor and a tray that tilts side to side. Mark eggs with an X and O to track turning. Keep the incubator in a room with stable temperature, away from direct sun and drafts. Clean and disinfect the incubator after each hatch. A homemade incubator can cost under $20 and hatch 80% of fertile eggs if managed well.

lessons.title: Step-by-Step Incubation: Temperature, Humidity, and Turning
lessons.body:
Set your incubator to 37.5Â°C (99.5Â°F) for forced-air or 38.5Â°C (101.3Â°F) for still-air incubators. Measure temperature at egg level, not at the top. Use two thermometers to be safe. Humidity should be 45-55% for the first 14 days for quail and first 24 days for guinea fowl. Fill the water channels or place a wet sponge. Check humidity daily and add warm water as needed. Never let the incubator dry out completely. If you live in a dry area, add a second water container. If it is too humid, reduce water surface area.

Turn eggs at least 4 times a day, ideally 6 times. Turn them 180 degrees each time. If you have an automatic turner, set it to turn every 2 hours. If turning by hand, mark one side X and the other O. Turn all X to O and O to X. Do not turn eggs during the last 3 days before hatch. For quail, stop turning on day 15; for guinea fowl, stop on day 25. This allows chicks to get into position for hatching. Keep the incubator closed during lockdown except to add water. Open it only if absolutely necessary.

Candling is optional but helps you remove infertile eggs. On day 7 for quail and day 10 for guinea fowl, shine a bright torch through the egg in a dark room. Fertile eggs show a spiderweb of blood vessels and a dark spot (embryo). Infertile eggs look clear. Remove clear eggs to prevent rotting. Keep records of temperature, humidity, and turning times. A simple notebook works. If temperature spikes above 39Â°C (102Â°F) for more than 30 minutes, embryos may die. If it drops below 35Â°C (95Â°F) for a few hours, development slows. Always have a backup power source or a plan to move eggs under a broody hen if electricity fails.

lessons.title: Candling Eggs to Check Fertility and Development
lessons.body:
Candling means shining a bright light through an egg to see inside. Do it in a dark room. Use a strong LED torch or a smartphone flashlight. Make a small cone from cardboard to focus the light. Hold the egg at the narrow end and shine the light through the wide end. For quail eggs, candle on day 5-7. For guinea fowl, candle on day 7-10. You can also candle again on day 14 for quail and day 20 for guinea fowl to check growth. Do not candle too often; each time you handle eggs, you risk damage.

A fertile egg at day 7 shows a network of red blood vessels like a spiderweb and a small dark dot (the embryo). You may see the embryo move if you are quick. An infertile egg looks clear like a fresh egg, with no veins. A dead embryo shows a blood ring (a circle of blood) or a cloudy mass with no veins. Remove infertile and dead eggs immediately. They rot and can explode, spreading bacteria and bad smell. Also remove cracked eggs. If you are not sure, wait 2 more days and candle again. A good candling light should not heat the egg too much; use LED, not incandescent.

Record your findings. If more than 20% of eggs are infertile, check your male-to-female ratio and feed. If many embryos die early, your temperature may be too high or low. If they die late, humidity might be wrong. Candling helps you learn and improve. After candling, return good eggs to the incubator quickly. Do not leave eggs out for more than 10 minutes. Wash your hands before and after handling eggs. Keep the candling area clean. With practice, you can candle 30 eggs in 15 minutes. This simple skill saves you from wasting incubator space and helps you hatch more chicks.

lessons.title: Hatch Day: Assisting Chicks and Managing the Brooder
lessons.body:
Hatch day for quail is day 17-18; for guinea fowl, day 26-28. On day 15 for quail or day 24 for guinea fowl, stop turning eggs and increase humidity to 65-75%. Do not open the incubator unless you must add water. You will hear peeping and tapping. Chicks pip a small hole in the shell, then rest for several hours. They then zip around the shell and push out. This can take 12-24 hours. Do not help a chick that is still pipping and active. Only assist if the chick has been stuck for more than 12 hours with no progress, and the membrane is dry and stuck to the chick. If you help too early, you can kill the chick by breaking blood vessels.

If you must assist, use clean hands and a small piece of warm, wet cloth. Gently peel away the shell from the pip hole, bit by bit. Stop if you see blood. Moisten the membrane with warm water. Let the chick do the rest. After hatching, leave chicks in the incubator until they are dry and fluffy, usually 6-12 hours. Then move them to a pre-warmed brooder. The brooder can be a cardboard box with a 60-watt bulb or a heat lamp. Set the temperature to 35Â°C (95Â°F) for the first week, then reduce by 3Â°C each week until it matches room temperature. Use a thermometer at chick level.

Line the brooder with clean, dry bedding like wood shavings or old towels. Do not use newspaper because it is slippery. Provide shallow water dishes with marbles or stones to prevent drowning. Feed chick starter crumbs or finely ground maize, millet, and boiled egg yolk. Quail chicks need 24-28% protein; guinea fowl chicks need 24% protein. Keep the brooder clean and dry. Change bedding daily. Watch for pasty butt (droppings stuck to the vent) and gently clean with warm water. Keep chicks away from drafts and other animals. After 2 weeks, quail chicks can be moved to a small cage; guinea fowl chicks need 4-6 weeks before going outside. Always provide fresh water and feed.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Incubation and Hatching Guinea Fowl & Quail â From Egg to Chick

In West, Central, and East Africa, day-old guinea keets and quail chicks sell at a premium because supply is unreliable and demand keeps rising â especially from restaurants, hotels, and health-conscious urban buyers who value quail meat and eggs. The bottleneck is almost never the adult birds; it is hatchability. A farmer who masters collection, storage, incubation, candling, and brooding can turn a small flock into a reliable chick business with low capital. This Practical Reference gives you the numbers, the timing, and the low-cost methods that work with locally available materials.

Two species, two very different incubation profiles. Guinea fowl eggs are thick-shelled and need slightly higher humidity and a longer window than chicken eggs. Quail eggs are small, highly pigmented, and hatch fast â often in 17â18 days for Japanese quail. Treating them the same is the most common cause of poor hatches on African smallholder farms.

1. Collecting and Storing Fertile Eggs

Collect eggs at least twice daily â morning and late afternoon â because African midday heat (30â38 Â°C) quickly damages the blastoderm. Never wash hatching eggs; the bloom protects against bacteria. If an egg is soiled, wipe with a dry, slightly abrasive cloth or fine sandpaper. Store eggs pointed-end down in clean egg trays at 15â18 Â°C and 70â80 % relative humidity for a maximum of 7 days for guinea fowl and 5â7 days for quail. Beyond 10 days, hatchability drops sharply. In hot climates, a cool dark room, a clay pot with damp sand, or an evaporative cooler works better than a refrigerator (which is too cold and too dry).

Turn stored eggs at least twice a day if kept longer than 3 days. Do not store near onions, kerosene, or strong-smelling chemicals â eggs absorb odours and this reduces hatch rates.

2. Natural Incubation with Local Hens or Guinea Fowl

A broody local hen can sit on 12â15 guinea fowl eggs or 20â25 quail eggs. Guinea fowl hens are notoriously unreliable sitters â they often abandon nests â so use a proven broody chicken or a Muscovy duck for guinea eggs. Quail eggs are best hatched under a small bantam hen or in an incubator; standard hens may crush them.

Set the nest in a quiet, dark, dry corner with soft bedding (dry grass, wood shavings). Feed the broody hen off the nest once daily and provide water nearby. Mark the eggs and remove any added by other hens. Expect guinea fowl to hatch in 26â28 days and quail in 17â18 days under a hen.

3. Building a Low-Cost Incubator with a Thermostat and Bulb

A simple still-air incubator can be built from a wooden box, a styrofoam cooler, or even a plastic drum lined with cardboard for insulation. You need: a 40â60 W incandescent bulb as heat source, a thermostat (e.g., a W1209 digital module), a small computer fan for forced-air models, a water tray for humidity, and a thermometer/hygrometer. Place the bulb at one end and the eggs at the other so heat is gentle, not direct.

Calibrate the thermostat for 2â3 days with a known-good thermometer before setting eggs. In many African markets, a W1209 thermostat costs less than a bag of feed and transforms hatch rates. Always wire through a fuse and keep the incubator off the floor and away from direct sun.

4. Step-by-Step Incubation: Temperature, Humidity, and Turning

For guinea fowl eggs: 37.5 Â°C (99.5 Â°F) in forced-air incubators, 38.3 Â°C (101 Â°F) in still-air, humidity 55â60 % during incubation and 65â75 % at hatch. For quail: 37.5 Â°C, humidity 50â55 % rising to 60â70 % at hatch. Turn eggs 3â5 times daily for the first 21 days (guinea) or 14 days (quail), then stop turning and raise humidity for lockdown.

Mark eggs with an X and O on opposite sides so you can confirm turning. In hot African climates, open ventilation holes during the day and close at night if temperatures drop. Never let the incubator exceed 39.5 Â°C â a single hour above this can kill embryos.

Table 1: Incubation parameters for guinea fowl and Japanese quail
ParameterGuinea FowlJapanese Quail
Incubation period26â28 days17â18 days
Temperature (forced-air)37.5 Â°C37.5 Â°C
Temperature (still-air)38.3 Â°C38.3 Â°C
Humidity (incubation)55â60 %50â55 %
Humidity (lockdown)65â75 %60â70 %
Turning stopsDay 24Day 14
Eggs per broody hen12â1520â25

Sources: FAO Small-scale poultry production (2004); Aviagen & Ross breeder guidelines (adapted); K. Nahashon et al., Journal of Applied Poultry Research on quail incubation.

5. Candling Eggs to Check Fertility and Development

Candle at day 5â7 (guinea) and day 4â5 (quail). In a dark room, hold a strong LED torch against the blunt end. Fertile eggs show a spider-web of blood vessels and a dark embryo. Clear eggs are infertile or early dead â remove them. A blood ring without vessels means early death. By day 14 (guinea) or day 10 (quail), the egg should be mostly dark with an air cell at the blunt end.

Quail eggshells are heavily pigmented, so use a very bright torch and cup your hand around the egg. Do not candle after day 18 for guinea or day 14 for quail â the risk of chilling or introducing bacteria outweighs the benefit.

6. Hatch Day: Assisting Chicks and Managing the Brooder

On hatch day, do not open the incubator unless absolutely necessary â humidity must stay high. Chicks that pip and rest for 12â24 hours are normal. Assist only if a chick has been stuck for more than 24 hours with dried membrane. Never pull a chick out of the shell. Once chicks are dry and fluffed (6â12 hours), move them to a pre-warmed brooder at 35 Â°C for quail and 32â35 Â°C for guinea keets, reducing by 2â3 Â°C weekly.

Provide clean water with a shallow dish and marbles or stones to prevent drowning, and a starter feed of 24â28 % protein crumbles. Guinea keets are highly susceptible to dampness â keep bedding dry and replace daily. Quail chicks grow fast; they need brooder space of about 50 cmÂ² per bird in week one.

Table 2: Brooding temperatures and key management by species
WeekGuinea keet tempQuail chick tempKey action
Week 132â35 Â°C35 Â°CWater + 24â28 % protein starter
Week 229â32 Â°C32 Â°CExpand space; dry bedding
Week 326â29 Â°C29 Â°CVaccinate (Newcastle) where available
Week 423â26 Â°C26 Â°CTransition to grower feed
Week 5+Ambient (if >20 Â°C)AmbientMove to grow-out pens

Sources: FAO Small-scale poultry production (2004); University of Kentucky Cooperative Extension, Quail production; Guinea Fowl International Association guidelines.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Electrical and Fire Risk

Home-made incubators using bulbs and thermostats are a leading cause of farm fires and electrocution in Africa. Always use a fused plug and an RCD/earth-leakage breaker. Keep wiring away from water trays. Never run an incubator on a bare extension lead or near curtains, bedding, or fuel. If you use a generator, install a surge protector. Do not touch bulbs, wiring, or water with wet hands. Unplug before cleaning or adjusting. Children must not have access to the incubator room unsupervised.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Collect eggs twice daily; never wash; store pointed-end down at 15â18 Â°C for â¤7 days.
  • Use a proven broody hen for guinea eggs (12â15) or bantam for quail (20â25).
  • Calibrate incubator thermostat for 2â3 days before setting eggs.
  • Guinea: 37.5 Â°C, 55â60 % RH, turn to day 24, hatch day 26â28.
  • Quail: 37.5 Â°C, 50â55 % RH, turn to day 14, hatch day 17â18.
  • Candle at day 5â7 (guinea) and day 4â5 (quail); remove clears.
  • Lockdown: stop turning, raise humidity, do not open the lid.
  • Brooder at 32â35 Â°C; dry bedding; 24â28 % protein starter; clean water.
  • Record every setting: date, temperature, humidity, turning, hatch rate â data drives profit.

Further Reading (Free Official Resources)

  • FAO â Small-scale poultry production: technical guide (2004): fao.org/3/y5169e
  • Practical Action â Small-scale poultry keeping: practicalaction.org
  • University of Kentucky Cooperative Extension â Quail production and incubation: uky.edu/Ag/AnimalSciences/pubs
  • International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) â Poultry in Africa: ilri.org
  • African Union â Livestock Development Strategy for Africa: au.int

Business takeaway: A farmer hatching 200 quail eggs every 18 days at a 70 % hatch rate produces 140 chicks. At a modest $0.80 per day-old quail chick, that is $112 per cycle â over $1,800 per year from one small incubator. Guinea keets sell even higher. Master the numbers in this module, keep clean records, and incubation stops being a gamble and becomes a repeatable, profitable production line.

quiz.q: What is the ideal male-to-female ratio for breeding quail or guinea fowl?
quiz.explanation: One male can mate with 3-5 females without stress, ensuring good fertility.

quiz.q: How should you clean a dirty hatching egg?
options: A) Wash with soap and water
B) Rub gently with fine sandpaper or dry cloth
quiz.explanation: Washing removes the protective bloom; dry rubbing cleans without damaging it.

quiz.q: What is the best storage temperature for hatching eggs?
quiz.explanation: Cool, stable temperatures between 15-20Â°C keep embryos alive but dormant.

quiz.q: How often should you turn stored eggs before incubation?
quiz.explanation: Turning at least twice a day prevents the embryo from sticking to the shell.

quiz.q: What is the maximum storage time for quail eggs before hatchability drops?
quiz.explanation: Quail eggs should be set within 7 days for best hatch rates.

quiz.q: Which bird is commonly used as a natural incubator for quail eggs?
quiz.explanation: Local hens are calm and can cover 15-20 quail eggs.

quiz.q: How many quail eggs can a local hen typically cover?
quiz.explanation: A hen's body size allows her to keep 15-20 small quail eggs warm.

quiz.q: What should you do when a broody hen leaves the nest?
options: C) Check for broken eggs and clean
quiz.explanation: Quickly remove broken eggs to prevent rot and bacteria.

quiz.q: How long does natural incubation take for quail eggs?
quiz.explanation: Quail eggs hatch in about 17-18 days under a hen or incubator.

quiz.q: What is a sign that a chick needs help hatching?
options: B) It has been stuck for over 12 hours with no progress
C) It is making loud noises
quiz.explanation: Only assist if the chick is truly stuck and membrane is dry.

quiz.q: What wattage bulb is recommended for a low-cost incubator?
quiz.explanation: Incandescent bulbs produce necessary heat; 40-60W is sufficient for small boxes.

quiz.q: What is the ideal incubation temperature for a forced-air incubator?
quiz.explanation: 37.5Â°C (99.5Â°F) is standard for forced-air incubators.

quiz.q: Why should you test an incubator for 24 hours before setting eggs?
options: B) To stabilise temperature and humidity
quiz.explanation: Testing ensures steady conditions before placing valuable eggs.

quiz.q: What humidity range is needed during the first 14 days of quail incubation?
quiz.explanation: 45-55% humidity prevents eggs from drying out too fast.

quiz.q: How often should eggs be turned by hand during incubation?
quiz.explanation: Turning 4-6 times daily mimics the hen's natural behaviour.

quiz.q: When should you stop turning eggs before hatch?
quiz.explanation: Lockdown 3 days before hatch allows chicks to position for hatching.

quiz.q: What does a fertile egg look like when candled on day 7?
options: B) Spiderweb of red blood vessels
D) Cloudy with a blood ring
quiz.explanation: Blood vessels and a dark embryo indicate fertility.

quiz.q: What should you do with an infertile egg after candling?
options: D) Put it under a hen
quiz.explanation: Infertile eggs rot and can explode, harming other eggs.

quiz.q: What does a blood ring in a candled egg indicate?
quiz.explanation: A blood ring means the embryo died early and should be removed.

quiz.q: How long should you candle eggs to avoid overheating them?
quiz.explanation: Quick candling prevents chilling or overheating the embryo.

quiz.q: What humidity is needed during lockdown (last 3 days)?
quiz.explanation: Higher humidity softens the shell for easier hatching.

quiz.q: What should you do if a chick is stuck but still active?
quiz.explanation: Active chicks usually hatch on their own; interfering can cause injury.

quiz.q: What temperature should a brooder be in the first week?
quiz.explanation: Chicks need 35Â°C (95Â°F) in week one, reduced by 3Â°C weekly.

quiz.q: What bedding is recommended for a brooder?
quiz.explanation: Wood shavings are absorbent and provide grip; newspaper is slippery.

quiz.q: What protein level do quail chicks need?
quiz.explanation: Quail chicks grow fast and need high protein for healthy development.

quiz.q: What is pasty butt in chicks?
options: B) Droppings stuck to the vent
quiz.explanation: Pasty butt blocks the vent and must be gently cleaned with warm water.

quiz.q: How long should chicks stay in the incubator after hatching?
quiz.explanation: Chicks need to dry and fluff up before moving to the brooder.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of natural incubation?
quiz.explanation: Natural incubation is low-cost and works without power.

quiz.q: What should you do if the incubator temperature spikes above 39Â°C?
quiz.explanation: Briefly opening the lid can cool it, but avoid prolonged exposure.

quiz.q: Why is record-keeping important in incubation?
options: B) To track and improve hatch rates
quiz.explanation: Records help identify problems like temperature or humidity issues.
